Learning Objective

   basic concepts of following topics used in learning application
   of AI to robotics

   – Probability and Statistics
   – Transforms and control
   – Graph theory and search algorithms
   – Complexity analysis

slides.title: Linear Algebra – Matrices (Cont.)
slides.text:
Linear Algebra – Matrices (Cont.)
•  Determinant, Rank, and Matrix Inverse
   – The determinant (det 𝐀) is a single number (a scalar) calculated from a
      square matrix. It tells whether a matrix is invertible or not. It acts as scaling
       factor for linear transformations.
   – Rank is the maximum number of linearly independent rows or columns in 𝐀
   – Matrix Inverse (𝐀−𝟏): Exists only if det 𝐀≠0             1                                     𝐀−𝟏=      adj 𝐀
       (non-singular matrix); satisfies 𝐀𝐀−𝟏= 𝐈                   det 𝐀
   – A Singularity occurs if the Jacobian matrix loses rank
       (det 𝐉= 0), making the inverse impossible to
      compute.
   – Calculating the joint angles required to reach a
        specific target position.

slides.title: Linear Algebra (Cont.)
slides.text:
Linear Algebra (Cont.)

•  Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors:
   – For a square matrix 𝐀, eigenvectors 𝒙 are non-zero vectors that satisfy
    𝐀𝒙= 𝜆𝒙, where 𝜆 is the eigenvalue.
   – The Characteristic Equation: det(𝜆𝐈−𝐀) = 0
   – They represent the principal directions and scaling factors of a linear
       transformation.
   – Analyzing system stability: a robotic control system is
       asymptotically stable if the real parts of the
       eigenvalues of the system matrix are all negative.

       matrix or vector composed of the derivatives of its individual elements.

      and orientation are functions of time.

slides.title: Probability – Foundations
slides.text:
Probability – Foundations
•  Definitions
   – Probability is a measure over a set of events (sample
      space Ω) satisfying specific axioms that quantify the
       likelihood of outcomes
                                    𝑛
      Axioms: 0 ≤𝑃𝑋≤𝑥𝑖≤1 and σ𝑖=1 𝑃𝑋= 𝑥𝑖= 1
   – An experiment (or trial) is a well-defined process of
       observation.
   – The sample space may be discrete (countable
      outcomes) or continuous (uncountable outcomes).
   – Determining the likelihood of a robot encountering a
        specific state (e.g., "path available?") in a discrete
      environment before taking any action.

Probability – Random Variables

•  Definition
   – A random variable 𝑋 is a function 𝑋: Ω →ℝ that maps experimental
      outcomes to real numbers.
   – Expected value (Mean): 𝐸(𝑋) = σ𝑥𝑖 𝑃(𝑋= 𝑥𝑖) (Discrete)
                     𝐸(𝑋) = ׬ ∞𝑥 𝑓𝑋(𝑥)𝑑𝑥 (Continuous)                         −∞
   – Discrete random variables use a Probability Mass Function (PMF), while
      continuous variables use a Probability Density Function (PDF), 𝑓𝑋(𝑥).
   – Calculating the "expected" reward a robot receives in
       Q-learning based on a weighted average of potential

slides.title: Probability and Statistics – Bayesian estimation
slides.text:
Probability and Statistics – Bayesian estimation

   – Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) finds the parameter values that
       best explain the observed data only.
   – Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimation improves MLE by incorporating
       prior knowledge about the parameters.
                      𝑃𝑠𝜇𝑚𝑃𝜇𝑚
          MAP = arg max 𝑃𝜇𝑚𝑠=
                                           𝑃(𝑠)
      𝑃𝜇𝑚𝑠: The probability of model given the observed data/signal s
      𝑃𝑠𝜇𝑚: likelihood of sensor measurements (The probability of
          observing signal given that model 𝜇𝑚 is true".
      𝑃𝜇𝑚: prior belief about the parameter, probability of model 𝜇𝑚
          before seeing the data s.
      𝑃𝑠: The total probability of the data s across all possible models

slides.title: Probability and Statistics – Bayesian estimation (Cont.)
slides.text:
Probability and Statistics – Bayesian estimation (Cont.)
•  Bayesian Updating
             •  Begin with an initial belief (prior)
             •  Each new sensor observation updates this belief
             •  The updated belief (posterior) becomes the new prior
•  Robot Sensor Example
   – A mobile robot estimates its distance to a wall using a noisy range sensor:
             •  MLE: estimates distance using only the latest measurements
             • MAP: combines new measurements with prior knowledge
                 (e.g., map information)
   – As more sensor data arrives, the robot’s estimate
      becomes more accurate and stable.
 •   Bayesian estimation allows robots to continuously refine sensor-
    based estimates by combining data with prior knowledge.

slides.title: Probability and Statistics – Information theory
slides.text:
Probability and Statistics – Information theory

•  Entropy
   – Entropy (H) is a measure of average uncertainty or the "information
       content" of a random variable.
         𝐻𝑋= −σ𝑝𝑥log2 𝑝(𝑥)
   – Entropy relates to "surprise"; higher surprise indicates higher entropy.
   –  It is used to measure the quality of robotic models—better models capture
     more structure and thus have lower entropy.
   – In Decision Trees, entropy measures the "impurity" of
      a data split to determine the most informative
       features for robot classification tasks.





                                                                                                          17

slides.title: Transforms and Control – State-Space Equations
slides.text:
Transforms and Control – State-Space Equations

•  State-Space Representation of Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) Systems
   – A mathematical model of a physical system as a set of input, output, and
       state variables related by first-order differential equations.
   – This representation is essential for multi-variable robotic systems.
   – A higher-order differential equation (e.g., a mass-spring-damper system) is
      broken down into a vector of first-order equations
       State Equation: ሶ𝒙𝒕= 𝐀𝒙𝒕+ 𝐁𝒖𝒕
      Output Equation: 𝒚𝒕= 𝐂 𝒙𝒕
   – Modeling the dynamics of a robot arm where 𝒙(𝒕)
       represents position and velocity.

slides.title: Graph Theory – Fundamentals
slides.text:
Graph Theory – Fundamentals

   – A graph is an abstract mathematical representation of a set of objects
       (nodes, 𝑉) connected by links (edges, 𝐸), denoted as 𝐺= (𝑉, 𝐸) .
   – Edges can be directed, indicating one-way traversal, or undirected. It
       represents the weight/cost to move between nodes
   – A sequence of edges from one node to another is a path, and a path that
        starts and ends at the same node is a cycle.
   – A tree is a specific type of connected directed graph that contains no cycles
      and has a root node.
   – Path Cost: The sum of the weights of all edges in a
      sequence {𝑉1, 𝑉2 , … , 𝑉𝑛}

slides.title: Graph Theory – Uninformed Search
slides.text:
Graph Theory – Uninformed Search

•  Uninformed searches explore a graph without any preference for
  the goal's location, relying solely on the graph's structure.
•  Breadth-First Search (BFS)
   – BFS: Explores all nodes at a specific link length (the number of edges from
      the start) before moving deeper.
             •  Implemented using a Queue (First-In, First-Out, FIFO) and guaranteed to find the shortest
            path in terms of the number of edges (not distance, cost, or heuristics).

slides.title: Graph Theory – Uninformed Search (Cont.)
slides.text:
Graph Theory – Uninformed Search (Cont.)

•  Depth-First Search (DFS)
   – Explores a path as deeply as possible before
       backtracking to unvisited children.
             •  Implemented using a Stack (Last-In, First-Out or
             LIFO) and is often more memory-efficient in deep
            graphs but does not guarantee an optimal path.
   – The highlighted DFS path is the first
       solution found, not necessarily the optimal
      one.
•  DFS is fast for exploration, BFS is better
  when the shortest path matters.

slides.title: Graph Theory – Search Trees
slides.text:
Graph Theory – Search Trees

• A search tree represents a sequence of decisions:
   – Internal nodes → questions or tests on attributes (e.g. Is the surface glass?)
   – Branches → outcomes of those tests (yes / no, high / low, etc.)
   – Leaf nodes → final decisions or classifications (e.g., fragile or sturdy)
•  This structure mirrors how decisions are made step by step.
•  They are commonly used for classification
   tasks, where sensor data must be mapped to an
   action or label.
    –  Decision Trees → one explicit set of decision rules
    – Random Forests → many decision trees combined for robustness

slides.title: Graph Theory – Search Trees (Cont.)
slides.text:
Graph Theory – Search Trees (Cont.)

   – The goal is to reduce uncertainty using Entropy.
             •  Entropy (H): 𝐻𝑋= −σ𝑝𝑥log2 𝑝𝑥
                    If the robot is unsure whether an object is fragile or sturdy,
            entropy is high.
             •  Information Gain: H(Parent)−∑P(Child)×H(Child).
           The robot chooses the attribute that gives the largest reduction
               in entropy. This determines the order of questions in the tree
   – A robot arm classifies an object as “fragile” or
       “sturdy” using visual sensors.
             •   If surface = glass → Fragile → apply low grasp force
             •  Else → check other properties (e.g., thickness) → decide grasp
              force
              This explicit decision logic improves safety, interpretability,
           and control.

slides.title: Complexity Analysis – Asymptotic Analysis and O() Notation
slides.text:
Complexity Analysis – Asymptotic Analysis and O() Notation

   – Complexity analysis studies how the number of steps an algorithm takes,
      denoted as 𝑇(𝑛), grows as the input size 𝑛 becomes very large.
   – Instead of measuring runtime on a specific computer, asymptotic analysis
       provides a hardware-independent way to compare algorithms.
   –  It focuses on the highest-order term of 𝑇(𝑛), since this term dominates
      performance for large inputs.
   – Example (Robot Path Planning):
             •  Algorithm A: 𝑇𝑛= 100𝑛+ 1000 (linear, O(n))
             •  Algorithm B: 𝑇(𝑛) = 𝑛2 + 1(Quadratic, O(𝑛2))
   – As the grid size increases, the linear algorithm scales
       better than the quadratic one, even if it has larger
       constants.

slides.title: Complexity Analysis – Running Time and Search Efficiency
slides.text:
Complexity Analysis – Running Time and Search Efficiency

   – Running time is a measure of the number of operations performed by an
       algorithm, typically categorized as worst-case or average-case.
   – In robotics, search algorithms like Breadth-First Search (BFS), Depth-First
      Search (DFS), and A* are analyzed for their efficiency.
   – BFS is uninformed but guaranteed to find an optimal path in terms of the
     number of edges, whereas A* uses a heuristic to improve search efficiency.
             • Common Running Times: Linear 𝑂(𝑛), Logarithmic 𝑂(log 𝑛), and Quadratic 𝑂(𝑛2)
    – A robot navigating a grid using the A* algorithm:
              •   If the robot uses Euclidean distance as its heuristic the search
                   is more efficient than BFS because it expands fewer nodes (O
                   is reduced in practice) by ignoring directions that move away
            from the goal

slides.title: Complexity Analysis - Algorithm Completeness
slides.text:
Complexity Analysis - Algorithm Completeness

   – Completeness characterizes whether an algorithm is guaranteed to find a
       solution if one exists
             •  Complete: Always finds a solution in finite time or determines that none exists (e.g., A*).
             •  Resolution Complete: Finds a solution if the discretization (grid resolution) is small
            enough.
             •  Probabilistically Complete: The probability of finding a solution converges to 1 as time
            approaches infinity.
   – Using a Genetic Algorithm for robot path planning.
             •  Genetic algorithms are often probabilistically complete
             •  They may find a near-optimal path quickly through random
             mutations, but unlike A*, they do not guarantee finding the
             absolute shortest path in a finite number of steps

slides.title: Summary
slides.text:
Summary

•   Linear Algebra: Vectors, matrices, eigenvalues, SVD, and Jacobians form the backbone
    of robot kinematics, dynamics, and control.
•   Calculus: Gradients, Jacobians, chain rule, and time derivatives enable motion analysis,
    velocity mapping, and dynamic modeling.
•   Probability & Statistics: Random variables, distributions, Bayesian estimation, and
   entropy support perception, localization, learning, and decision-making under
    uncertainty.
•  Transforms & Control: State-space models
•  Graph Theory & Search: BFS, DFS, and decision trees power
   path planning, navigation, and sequential decision-making.
•  Complexity Analysis: Big-O notation, complexity classes, and
   completeness guide algorithm selection and performance
    evaluation.
